title: AI Unlocked: Education
blurb: For teachers, lecturers, and school leaders: lesson planning and differentiation at speed, the honest academic-integrity playbook, a head-to-head study of teacher AI platforms, and an AI-literacy unit you can teach next term.

modules.d: AI won't replace teachers — but teachers who use AI will redefine the profession. Your new role.
modules.body:
The question every teacher is asking — answered honestly

"Will AI replace teachers?" No — but it will transform what teaching is. The parts of the job a machine can do (drafting, differentiating, grading routine work, generating materials) are being automated. The parts only a human can do (inspiring, mentoring, reading a child's face, building character) become more valuable, not less. The AI-era educator offloads the mechanical and pours the reclaimed time into what actually changes lives. This course makes you that educator.

"Technology will not replace great teachers, but technology in the hands of great teachers can be transformational." — George Couros. AI is the most powerful such technology yet — and it lands in your hands, not over your head.

What AI gives back to teachers: time

Teacher burnout is largely a time problem — hours lost to prep, paperwork, and grading that never touch a student. AI is, above all, a time machine for educators:

  • Lesson planning in minutes, aligned to your curriculum and objectives.
  • Differentiation — the same lesson instantly leveled for different readers and needs.
  • Materials — worksheets, quizzes, examples, rubrics, parent letters — on demand.
  • Feedback — faster, richer, more consistent (with your judgment on top).
  • Admin — emails, reports, and documentation drafted for you.

Reclaim those hours and spend them where the magic is: with students.

The educator's non-negotiables (Commandments, applied to teaching)

  • You are the professional. AI drafts; you decide. Every material is checked by your expertise and judgment before it reaches a student.
  • Accuracy matters doubly in education. A hallucinated fact taught as truth is a real harm. Verify — Commandment 2 is sacred in the classroom.
  • Protect students. Never put student personal data or identifiable work into public AI tools without consent and care (Module 3 goes deep). Do no harm.
  • Model good use. How you use AI teaches your students how they should — integrity, transparency, and thinking with the tool, not outsourcing to it.
The mindset shift: stop seeing AI as either a threat to resist or a cheat to fear. See it as a tireless teaching assistant who preps, differentiates, and drafts on command — while you remain the teacher who inspires, judges, and cares. The assistant handles the mechanical so the human can be more human.

🧪 Validated exercise

AI's greatest gift to teachers is best described in one word:

Going deeper — what the evidence says about AI in classrooms

Early research on AI in learning shows a consistent pattern: design decides outcomes. A widely cited field experiment in Turkish high schools (Bastani et al.) found that students given unrestricted access to a GPT-4 tutor performed better during practice but worse on later exams without it than students who never had it, while a version designed with teacher-written hints that withheld direct answers largely avoided that harm. A World Bank–supported after-school pilot in Nigeria, where students used AI with teacher guidance, reported substantial learning gains over six weeks. The lesson: AI that gives answers can replace thinking; AI designed to prompt thinking can support it.

  • Productive struggle: learning needs effort. Design AI use so students attempt first and get hints, not solutions.
  • Teacher in the loop: the strongest results come when teachers frame tasks, set guardrails and debrief.
  • Equity: unequal access to devices and connectivity can widen gaps. Plan for offline and shared-device options.
UNESCO guidance recommends a human-centred approach, age-appropriate use, data protection, and building teacher capacity before scaling. Check your national and school policies too.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are an instructional designer. I teach [subject, level, setting]. Design one AI-supported activity that requires students to attempt the task first, then use AI only for hints, then explain their reasoning without AI. Include the student-facing prompt rules, a no-device alternative, and how I'll debrief.

📚 Glossary

  • Productive struggle: Effortful thinking that builds durable learning
  • Teacher in the loop: Teacher designs, guides and reviews AI use
  • Digital divide: Unequal access to devices and connectivity
  • Human-centred AI: Using AI to support, not replace, human agency

📖 References

  • Bastani, H. et al. (2024/2025). Generative AI can harm learning. Working paper; published in PNAS (2025) as 'Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning'.
  • De Simone, M. et al. (2025). From chalkboards to chatbots: evaluating the impact of generative AI on learning outcomes in Nigeria. World Bank Policy Research Working Paper.
  • UNESCO (2023). Guidance for generative AI in education and research.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Offload the mechanical, protect the human. The clearer you are on this line, the more AI helps without hollowing out your craft.
  • You are always the professional. AI drafts; your expertise decides what reaches a child.
  • Model integrity. How you use AI quietly teaches your students how they should.

📚 Glossary

  • Differentiation: adapting the same content to different learners' levels and needs.
  • AI-era educator: a teacher who offloads mechanical work to focus on human impact.
  • Human-in-the-loop: teacher judgment reviewing every AI output.

📖 Explore further

  • UNESCO — AI in education guidance.
  • Ethan Mollick & Lilach Mollick on teaching with AI — One Useful Thing.

modules.d: Turn hours of prep into minutes — curriculum-aligned lessons, leveled for every learner.
modules.body:
Where AI saves teachers the most time

Lesson planning and differentiation are the biggest, most repetitive time-sinks in teaching — and where AI delivers the most dramatic relief. This module gives you reusable workflows (not one-off tricks) that turn an evening of prep into a few minutes of directing and reviewing. Build these once and use them every week for the rest of your career.

Workflow 1 — The curriculum-aligned lesson plan

The key is giving AI your real context, not a generic ask. A strong lesson-plan prompt includes: the topic, the grade/level, your learning objectives (ideally your exact curriculum standards), the time available, your students' context, and the format you want. Feed all of that and you get a plan you can actually teach — then you refine it with your judgment.

Objectives first. The single biggest quality lever is giving AI your specific learning objectives or standards. "Plan a lesson on fractions" is weak. "Plan a 45-minute lesson for Grade 5 meeting objective [X: compare fractions with unlike denominators], with a hook, guided practice, and an exit ticket" is a plan you can walk into class with.

Workflow 2 — Instant differentiation

This is AI's superpower for inclusive teaching. Take one lesson or text and instantly adapt it:

  • By reading level: "Rewrite this passage at three levels — below, at, and above grade — keeping the same core content."
  • For support needs: "Adapt this for a student who needs simpler language and shorter chunks."
  • For extension: "Add two challenge questions for students who finish early."
  • For language learners: "Provide a version with key vocabulary defined in simple terms."
  • By interest: "Reframe these word problems around football / music / cooking to boost engagement."

What used to mean writing three versions of everything by hand now takes one prompt — real differentiation becomes finally achievable for a busy teacher.

Workflow 3 — The materials factory

From one lesson, generate the whole supporting set: a worksheet, a short quiz, a rubric, worked examples, discussion questions, and a parent update — all aligned and on demand. Save your best prompts (Level 2's prompt library) so next week is even faster.

"Differentiation is the hardest thing we ask of teachers, and the first thing that gets cut when time runs out." AI removes the time barrier — for the first time, meeting every learner where they are is realistic on a normal teaching schedule.

🧪 Lesson-plan lab (copy → run to plan a real lesson)

You are an expert instructional designer. Plan a [duration] lesson on [topic] for [grade/level]. Learning objective(s): [your exact standard/objective]. Student context: [class size, needs, language]. Include: a hook, direct instruction, guided practice, an independent task, and an exit ticket. Then differentiate the independent task into three versions (below / at / above level), and list the materials I'll need. Ask me one clarifying question first if anything essential is missing.

Going deeper — differentiation that respects learners

AI makes it easy to produce three versions of every task. Use that power carefully:

  • Differentiate access, not expectations. Adjust reading level, scaffolds, vocabulary support and format, while keeping the same core learning objective for all. Permanently giving some students easier goals can lower attainment.
  • Universal Design for Learning (UDL): offer multiple means of engagement, representation and expression — e.g. a diagram plus text, choice of written or oral response.
  • Avoid labels: don't name tiers "low/high". Use neutral labels or let students choose their starting scaffold.
  • Check accuracy and bias: simplified texts can drop key facts or introduce errors; AI examples may default to cultural contexts unfamiliar to your students. Localise names, currencies and settings.
Prompt pattern: "Create three versions of this reading for grade 7: one at a grade-5 reading level with a glossary, one at grade level, one with an extension question. Keep the same key facts and the same learning objective: [objective]. Use Cameroonian names and settings." Then check each version against the original.

Curriculum alignment

Always paste the actual curriculum objective or competency statement. Without it, AI plans drift toward generic content that may not match your national programme or exam.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a curriculum specialist. Here is my national curriculum objective: [paste]. Create a lesson plan with a starter, main activity, three differentiated access versions (same objective), a UDL option for expression, a quick formative check, and local examples from [country]. Then list anything I must verify for accuracy.

📚 Glossary

  • Differentiation: Adapting instruction to learners' needs
  • UDL: Universal Design for Learning: multiple means of engagement, representation and expression
  • Scaffold: Temporary support that helps learners reach a goal
  • Formative check: A quick assessment during learning to guide teaching

📖 References

  • CAST (2024). Universal Design for Learning Guidelines 3.0. udlguidelines.cast.org

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Objectives are the quality lever. Paste your exact standards; generic asks give generic lessons.
  • Build a workflow, not a one-off. Save your best planning and differentiation prompts to reuse weekly.
  • Differentiation is finally realistic. One prompt replaces three hand-written versions — use it every lesson.

📚 Glossary

  • Learning objective/standard: the specific skill a lesson targets.
  • Exit ticket: a quick end-of-lesson check of understanding.
  • Differentiation: adapting content to different learners.
  • Materials factory: generating a full aligned set from one lesson.

📖 Explore further

  • Teacher-focused tools (verify current features): MagicSchool, Diffit, Khanmigo, Brisk.
  • Level 2's prompt-library habit makes these workflows compound.

modules.t: Tool Study: The Teacher Platform Shoot-Out
modules.d: MagicSchool, Diffit, Khanmigo, NotebookLM and the general models — what each wins at, and when.
modules.body:
The teacher's AI toolkit (2025–26)

Beyond the general chatbots, a whole category of education-specific AI tools has emerged, built around teacher workflows and (crucially) student-data safety. This module maps the landscape so you pick the right tool per job. Tools evolve fast — verify current features, pricing, and privacy terms before adopting one for real student use.

Purpose-built teacher platforms

  • MagicSchool: a broad teacher suite — dozens of tools for planning, materials, feedback, IEP support, and more, designed around school workflows and privacy. Great one-stop starting point.
  • Diffit: specializes in exactly Module 1's superpower — take any text/topic and instantly generate leveled reading passages with questions and vocabulary. A differentiation powerhouse.
  • Khanmigo (Khan Academy): an AI tutor for students and a teaching aid, notable for a Socratic style that guides learners rather than handing answers — and for its safety-first design.
  • Brisk / others: browser-extension tools that work on top of Google Docs/Classroom for feedback and material creation inside the platforms teachers already use.

The general tools, in a teaching role

  • Claude / ChatGPT / Gemini: maximum flexibility for planning, drafting, and ideation — your CLEAR prompting makes them do almost anything. Best when a purpose-built tool doesn't fit.
  • NotebookLM: grounded Q&A over YOUR sources — upload the textbook chapter and curriculum, and get cited, on-syllabus answers and study aids (including audio overviews for revision). Excellent for accuracy.
  • Canva / Ideogram: visuals, posters, and slide design for engaging materials.
"Purpose-built for privacy" is the phrase that matters in education. The reason to prefer a teacher platform over a raw chatbot for student work isn't features — it's that it's designed to handle student data responsibly. Module 3 makes this non-negotiable.
Choosing fast — a teacher's decision rule: leveled reading passages → Diffit. A broad all-in-one with privacy → MagicSchool. A guided student tutor → Khanmigo. Cited answers from your own textbook → NotebookLM. Open-ended planning & drafting → a general model (Claude/ChatGPT/Gemini). Anything involving identifiable student data → a tool cleared by your school's privacy policy, never a random free app.

🧪 Validated exercise

The main reason to prefer a teacher platform over a raw chatbot for student work is student-data ___.

Going deeper — student data privacy and age rules

Before using any AI tool with students, check three things:

  • Age requirements: many general chatbots set minimum ages (often 13, with parental consent required below 18 for some services). Purpose-built education platforms may offer student accounts designed for younger learners under school control.
  • Data protection: in the US, FERPA and COPPA govern student records and children's data; in Europe, GDPR applies with stricter rules for children; Cameroon's 2024 law on personal data protection also sets obligations. Check whether the vendor signs a data agreement, whether student data trains models, and where data is stored.
  • Teacher-facing vs student-facing: a tool used only by teachers to plan (no student data entered) carries much lower risk than one where students log in or upload work.
Never paste student names, grades, special needs details or behaviour records into a consumer chatbot. Anonymise: "Student A, grade 8, reading two years below grade level".

Evaluating a teacher platform

Score candidates on: curriculum fit, output quality (test five real tasks), privacy terms, cost and offline access, language support (English/French), and whether it saves you time after review. Free tiers and features change often — recheck before committing a school.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a school data protection adviser. Here is a teacher AI tool I want to use and how: [tool, who uses it, what data]. Check it against minimum age rules, FERPA/COPPA or GDPR principles (and Cameroon's personal data law if relevant), identify what student data is involved, and give me a safe-use protocol for my classroom.

📚 Glossary

  • FERPA: US law protecting student education records
  • COPPA: US law on online data from children under 13
  • Teacher-facing tool: Tool used only by teachers, without student data
  • Data agreement: Contract governing how a vendor handles student data

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Verify privacy terms first. Before any tool touches student data, confirm it's cleared by your school's policy.
  • Diffit for differentiation, NotebookLM for accuracy. Two specialists worth learning well.
  • Don't over-collect tools. One all-in-one plus one grounded tool covers most teachers.

📚 Glossary

  • Purpose-built ed-tech: AI tools designed for teacher workflows and data safety.
  • Grounded answers: responses cited from your own sources (NotebookLM).
  • Socratic tutor: guides via questions rather than giving answers.

📖 Explore further

  • Verify directly: MagicSchool · Diffit · Khanmigo · NotebookLM.
  • Always check your school/district's approved-tools list.

modules.d: Faster, richer feedback — plus honest strategies for a world where students have AI too.
modules.body:
Two hard problems AI reshapes at once

Assessment is where AI both helps teachers enormously (faster, richer feedback) and creates a genuine challenge (students have AI too). This module handles both honestly: how to use AI to give better feedback, and how to design assessment with integrity in the AI era — not by fighting a losing detection war, but by rethinking what and how we assess.

AI-assisted feedback (with you in charge)

  • Faster first-pass feedback: "Give specific, encouraging feedback on this essay against this rubric, noting two strengths and two priorities." You then personalize and verify — the human touch stays yours.
  • Consistency: AI applies a rubric evenly across a class, reducing fatigue-driven drift — you spot-check and adjust.
  • Richer than a grade: generate actionable next steps, not just a score — what to do to improve, specifically.
  • Feedback in students' language: translate or simplify feedback for language learners.
The line you never cross: AI can draft feedback and apply a rubric, but the teacher owns the final judgment — especially for high-stakes grades and anything on a permanent record. And never paste identifiable student work into a non-approved tool (Module 2's privacy rule). AI assists the feedback; you remain the assessor.

Academic integrity: stop fighting, start redesigning

AI detectors are unreliable and produce false accusations — a dead end. The durable answer is to design assessment that AI can't simply do for the student, and to teach honest AI use openly:

  • Assess the process, not just the product: drafts, outlines, revisions, and reflections show the thinking AI can't fake for them.
  • In-class and oral components: discussion, presentation, and live explanation reveal genuine understanding.
  • Make it personal and local: tasks tied to a student's own experience, your specific classroom, or current local context are hard to outsource.
  • Raise the cognitive bar: ask for analysis, critique, application, and synthesis — not retrieval a chatbot hands over.
  • Teach AI use openly: set clear, honest rules for when and how AI may be used, and require students to disclose it — turning a threat into a skill.
"If an AI can complete your assignment perfectly, the problem may be the assignment." — a hard but freeing truth. The AI era is pushing assessment toward what always mattered most: thinking, process, and understanding over regurgitation.
🧪 Interactive Lab — AI-resilient assessment or not?

Oral defense of your own project
A reflection on your own drafting process
“Write a generic 500-word essay on photosynthesis at home”
“Define these ten terms” as take-home
Verdict
AI-resilient (shows real thinking)
AI-resilient (shows real thinking)

🧪 Redesign lab (copy → run on one of your assignments)

You are an assessment-design expert for the AI era. Here is one of my current assignments: [paste it]. First, tell me honestly how easily a student could complete it with AI. Then redesign it to assess genuine understanding — incorporating process (drafts/reflection), a personal or local element, and a higher-order thinking demand (analysis/critique/application) — while keeping it fair and doable. Finally, suggest a clear, honest AI-use policy statement I can put on the assignment.

Going deeper — why detectors fail and what works instead

AI-text detectors are unreliable for high-stakes decisions. OpenAI withdrew its own classifier in 2023 for low accuracy, and a Stanford study (Liang et al.) found detectors misclassified a large share of essays by non-native English writers as AI-generated. Accusing a student based on a detector score risks serious unfairness.

  • Assess process, not just product: drafts, outlines, version history, in-class writing and short oral check-ins ("talk me through your argument").
  • Set clear AI-use levels per task: e.g. an AI Assessment Scale ranging from no AI, to AI for planning, to AI for editing, to full AI collaboration with reflection. Students should know exactly what's allowed.
  • Design authentic tasks: local data, personal experience, recent events, and applied problems are harder to outsource.
  • Require AI disclosure: a short statement of what AI was used for and how the student checked it.
Feedback with AI, decisions by you. AI can draft rubric-aligned comments quickly, but teachers should review every comment and keep grading decisions human. Students value feedback that shows the teacher read their work.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are an assessment designer. Here is an assignment I set: [paste]. Redesign it for the AI era: specify the permitted AI-use level, add one process checkpoint and a short oral check-in, make it more authentic using local context, and write the student AI-disclosure statement. Then draft a rubric with four criteria.

📚 Glossary

  • AI detector: Tool that estimates whether text was AI-generated; unreliable for decisions
  • AI Assessment Scale: Framework defining permitted levels of AI use per task
  • Authentic assessment: Tasks rooted in real contexts and applied problems
  • Process evidence: Drafts, notes and history showing how work was produced

📖 References

  • Liang, W. et al. (2023). GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers. Patterns.
  • Perkins, M., Furze, L., Roe, J. & MacVaugh, J. (2024). The AI Assessment Scale. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Don't rely on detectors. They're unreliable and risk false accusations — redesign instead.
  • Assess the process. Drafts, reflections, and oral defenses reveal thinking AI can't fake for a student.
  • Teach honest use openly. Clear rules plus disclosure turn AI from a threat into a taught skill.

📚 Glossary

  • Formative feedback: guidance to improve, not just a grade.
  • AI-resilient assessment: tasks that require genuine, hard-to-outsource thinking.
  • Process assessment: grading drafts, revisions, and reflection.
  • AI-use policy: explicit rules for when/how students may use AI.

📖 Explore further

  • Level 1's integrity Commandments and Level 2's judgment principles apply directly.
  • UNESCO & university teaching centers publish evolving AI-integrity guidance — check current best practice.

modules.d: Your students will live and work with AI — prepare them to use it wisely, critically, and ethically.
modules.body:
The most important thing you'll teach this decade

Your students will spend their entire lives and careers alongside AI. Teaching them to use it wisely, critically, and ethically may be the most consequential thing you do — more lasting than any single subject. AI literacy isn't a computing topic; it's a life skill, like reading or reasoning, and every teacher in every subject can build it. This module shows how.

"We are not preparing students for our past; we are preparing them for their future." That future is saturated with AI. A student who can direct AI thoughtfully — and spot its failures — holds a decisive advantage; one who can't is left behind. You decide which your students become.

The four pillars of student AI literacy

  • Understanding (what AI is): age-appropriately, that AI is a powerful pattern-tool trained on data — not magic, not a person, not always right. Demystify it.
  • Critical evaluation (trust wisely): the vital habit of questioning AI output — checking for hallucinations, bias, and missing perspectives. This is the new critical thinking.
  • Effective use (direct it well): basic prompting and knowing which tasks AI helps with — and which need a human. Your own CLEAR skills, taught down to their level.
  • Ethical use (do right): honesty about when AI was used, respecting others' work, protecting privacy, and understanding fairness and bias. Character in the AI age.

How to build it in ANY subject

  • History: have AI write an account, then students fact-check and find its bias — critical evaluation in action.
  • Science: use AI to generate a hypothesis or explanation, then test and critique it.
  • Language arts: co-write with AI, then discuss what the student added that AI couldn't — voice, truth, experience.
  • Any subject: "AI got this wrong — find the error" is a powerful, transferable exercise that builds healthy skepticism.
The teach-the-limits principle: the single most valuable AI-literacy lesson is showing students where AI fails — the confident hallucination, the biased answer, the missing viewpoint. A student who expects AI to be fallible uses it wisely; one who trusts it blindly is vulnerable. Make "check it" a reflex.
🧪 Interactive Lab — Match the activity to the literacy pillar
Activity
Explain that AI is a data-trained pattern tool, not magic
Fact-check an AI account and find its bias
Practice writing a clear prompt
Disclose honestly when AI was used
Pillar
Understanding
Critical evaluation
Effective use
Ethical use

🧪 Literacy-lesson lab (copy → run to design an activity)

You are a curriculum designer for AI literacy. Design a [duration] activity for my [grade/subject] class that builds one AI-literacy pillar — [understanding / critical evaluation / effective use / ethical use]. Tie it to my subject content: [topic]. Include a hook, the student task, a “find where AI got it wrong” element to build healthy skepticism, and a short discussion to close. Keep it age-appropriate and doable with the tools I have.

Going deeper — a progression for AI literacy

AI literacy frameworks (UNESCO's AI competency framework for students, 2024; the joint EU/OECD AI literacy framework draft, 2025) converge on a few strands. Build them progressively:

  • Understand: AI learns patterns from data; it predicts, it doesn't "know". It can be wrong, biased and confident at the same time.
  • Use: prompt clearly, iterate, and choose when AI helps and when it doesn't.
  • Evaluate: verify claims against sources; spot hallucinations, bias and deepfakes.
  • Create: make things with AI responsibly — with attribution and disclosure.
  • Reflect on ethics and society: privacy, fairness, jobs, environmental cost, and who benefits.
Unplugged activities work. Students act as a "language model" predicting the next word from a pile of sentences; a "biased training set" sorting game using only pictures of one group; a fact-check race against an AI answer. No devices needed, and the concepts stick.

Age guidance

Younger students: concepts and unplugged activities, teacher-led demonstrations. Lower secondary: guided use with clear rules and verification tasks. Upper secondary: independent use with disclosure, critical projects on AI in society. Follow your school's and tools' age policies.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are an AI literacy curriculum designer. My students are [age, subject, setting, device access]. Design a four-lesson mini-unit covering understand, use, evaluate, create and ethics, including at least one unplugged activity, one verification challenge, and one discussion on AI in our local community. Include learning objectives and a final task.

📚 Glossary

  • AI literacy: Knowledge and skills to understand, use and evaluate AI responsibly
  • Unplugged activity: Teaching a computing concept without devices
  • Deepfake: Synthetic media realistic enough to deceive
  • Training data: Examples a model learns patterns from

📖 References

  • UNESCO (2024). AI competency framework for students.
  • European Commission & OECD (2025). Empowering learners for the age of AI: an AI literacy framework (draft).

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Teach the limits first. “Find where AI got it wrong” builds the skepticism that protects students for life.
  • Any subject can build literacy. You don't need a computing class — history, science, and language arts all work.
  • Model it yourself. Your transparent, critical AI use is the most powerful lesson of all.

📚 Glossary

  • AI literacy: understanding, critically evaluating, using, and ethically applying AI.
  • Critical evaluation: questioning AI output for errors, bias, and gaps.
  • Healthy skepticism: expecting AI to be fallible and checking it.

📖 Explore further

  • UNESCO — AI competency frameworks for students.
  • Level 1's data & vocabulary modules translate directly into student lessons.

modules.body:
Bring it all together for your real classroom

Your capstone isn't theoretical — it's a real, usable teaching artifact you'll actually deploy: a complete unit, a set of workflows, or a classroom AI system built with everything from this course. The test is simple: does it save you time, serve your students better, and uphold integrity and privacy? If yes, you've become an AI-era educator — and you have the materials to prove it.

Choose your capstone track

  • The Complete Unit: a full multi-lesson unit — curriculum-aligned plans, differentiated materials for at least three learner levels, AI-assisted feedback tools, and an AI-resilient assessment with an honest AI-use policy.
  • The Teacher Workflow System: your reusable prompt library and toolkit for planning, differentiation, materials, and feedback — documented so a colleague could adopt it.
  • The AI-Literacy Mini-Course: a sequence of activities that builds all four literacy pillars in your students, tied to your subject.
  • The Inclusive Classroom Kit: a differentiation system that adapts your core content for every learner — language, level, and need.

Capstone requirements

  • Real and usable — something you'll actually use, not a demo.
  • Curriculum-aligned — tied to your real objectives/standards.
  • Genuine differentiation — evidence of meeting varied learners.
  • Integrity & privacy by design — an AI-use policy and safe handling of student data (Modules 2–3).
  • Your prompt log — the CLEAR prompts you used, with iterations — proving the transferable skill.
  • A short reflection — what it saves you, how it helps students, and where you kept human judgment central.
"The teacher who uses AI won't replace the teacher who doesn't — but they will redefine what's possible in a classroom." Your capstone is that redefinition made concrete: more time for students, better support for every learner, and integrity intact.
🎓 Certification. Passing every module (75%+) and completing your capstone earns the AI Unlocked: Education certificate — a print-ready PDF with a QR validation code, signed by Innocent Forteh, Program Director, Team21 Academy. Each module also carries its own certificate in your Certificates tab.
Lead onward. Take these skills further with Level 2 OPERATE (build automations and systems for your whole school), Vibe Coding (build a custom classroom tool), or the Servant Leadership program (lead other educators through the AI transition). The AI-era educator is also an AI-era leader.
🧪 Capstone planner (copy → run to design your unit/system)

You are my capstone advisor for an AI-enabled classroom. My context: [grade, subject, class, constraints]. Help me choose the strongest track (complete unit, workflow system, AI-literacy mini-course, or inclusive kit). Then build a plan: the curriculum objectives it targets, how it differentiates for at least three learner levels, the AI-assisted feedback approach, an AI-resilient assessment with an honest AI-use policy, and how I'll protect student privacy. Finish with exactly what my finished, usable submission must contain.

🧪 Validated exercise

A capstone must protect student data — handling privacy and integrity by ___.

Going deeper — proving your capstone works

A capstone that "saves time and serves students better" must show evidence of both. Plan a simple before/after:

  • Time: log planning and marking time for one week without your AI workflow and one week with it (including review time).
  • Learning: use a short pre-check and post-check aligned to the unit objective, or compare with a similar previous class. Even small samples, honestly reported, are valuable.
  • Student voice: three questions — what helped, what confused you, how did you use AI? Their answers often reveal integrity or access issues you missed.
  • Integrity and privacy check: confirm no identifiable student data went into non-approved tools, and that each task states its AI-use level.
Make it shareable. Package your capstone so a colleague could use it tomorrow: a one-page overview, the prompts (with variables), materials, the AI-use rules for students, and your evidence. Sharing builds your reputation as the school's AI lead.

Reflection prompts

What did AI do well? Where did you overrule it? Which students benefited most and least, and why? What will you change next term?

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a teacher-researcher mentor. Here is my AI-enabled unit and the evidence I collected (time logs, pre/post checks, student comments): [paste]. Summarise the evidence honestly, identify which students benefited most and least, check the integrity and privacy safeguards, and suggest one change for next term.

📚 Glossary

  • Pre/post check: Short assessments before and after a unit to measure learning
  • Student voice: Students' own feedback on their learning experience
  • Net time saved: Time saved minus time spent reviewing AI output
  • Teacher-researcher: Teacher who systematically studies their own practice

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Build what you'll actually use. A real next-unit beats an impressive hypothetical.
  • Your prompt log is the proof. It shows the transferable skill, not just the output.
  • Design integrity in. An AI-use policy and safe data handling are requirements, not extras.

📚 Glossary

  • Capstone: the real, usable teaching artifact that completes the course.
  • By design: integrity and privacy built in from the start.
  • Prompt log: your documented, iterated CLEAR prompts.

📖 Explore further

  • Continue with Level 2, Vibe Coding, or Servant Leadership.
  • Share your capstone with the Team21 community — team21online@gmail.com.
